title.en: Lean Objects: __slots__ and Memory per Instance

description.en: Every ordinary Python object carries a hidden dictionary for its attributes. When you create a million small records, that dictionary is most of the cost. Measure it, then remove it with __slots__.

story_variants.en:
## The Hidden Dictionary

A normal class stores each object's attributes in a dictionary called `__dict__`. It is wonderfully flexible — you can add `p.colour = "red"` to any object at any time — and that flexibility costs memory on every instance.

```python
class Particle:
    def __init__(self, x, y, mass):
        self.x, self.y, self.mass = x, y, mass

hasattr(Particle(1, 2, 3), "__dict__")     # True
```

If you create a handful of objects, nobody cares. If you create **a million small records** — particles, rows, graph nodes, events — it adds up.

### Declare the fields up front

`__slots__` tells Python *exactly* which attributes the class has, so it can store them in fixed positions inside the object instead of a dictionary:

```python
class Particle:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y", "mass")
    def __init__(self, x, y, mass):
        self.x, self.y, self.mass = x, y, mass
```

Same code to use, but now there is no `__dict__`, and assigning an undeclared attribute raises `AttributeError` — a typo like `p.mas = 1` is caught instead of silently creating a new field.

Since Python 3.10 a dataclass can do it for you: `@dataclass(slots=True)`.

### What it really saves (measured)

We built 100,000 instances of each version on Python 3.11 and asked `tracemalloc` how much memory they held:

| Version | Memory for 100,000 instances |
|---|---|
| plain class, 3 attributes | about 10.4 MB (~104 bytes each) |
| `__slots__`, 3 attributes | about 6.4 MB (~64 bytes each) |

Roughly **40% less** here. Your numbers will differ with the Python version and the number of attributes, so measure your own case rather than trusting ours.

### The catches

- You lose dynamic attributes — fine for records, wrong for objects that need to grow fields.
- A subclass that doesn't declare its own `__slots__` gets a `__dict__` again, undoing the saving.
- It saves *memory* first; attribute access speed changes only a little. Don't add it to a class you create ten of.

> **Vaathiyaar's note:** use `__slots__` for many small, fixed-shape objects. Everywhere else, the plain class is the better default.

Your turn: add `__slots__` to `Particle` so its instances have no `__dict__`. The program should then print `False`.

explanation.en: A plain class: every instance gets its own __dict__.
Declare the field names once, on the class.
Instances store the three values in fixed slots.
There is no per-object dictionary any more: False.

instruction.en: `Particle` stores `x`, `y` and `mass`, and every instance carries a hidden `__dict__`. Add `__slots__` declaring exactly those three names so instances no longer have one. A hidden check confirms the attributes still read and write, that `p.__dict__` no longer exists, and that assigning an undeclared attribute raises `AttributeError`. The program must print `False`.

practice_challenges.starter_code:
class Particle:
    """A tiny record we will create in huge numbers."""
    def __init__(self, x, y, mass):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.mass = mass

p = Particle(1.0, 2.0, 0.5)
# Every Particle carries its own hidden attribute dictionary (__dict__).
print(hasattr(p, "__dict__"))

en: `__slots__` goes in the class body, before `__init__`.
It is a tuple of attribute names as strings: `("x", "y", "mass")`.
Don't remove the `self.x = x` lines — the slots only reserve the storage.
Declare exactly the three names; a typo in a slot name breaks `__init__`.

practice_challenges.test_code:
p = Particle(1.0, 2.0, 0.5)
assert (p.x, p.y, p.mass) == (1.0, 2.0, 0.5), "the three attributes must still work"
p.x = 9.0
assert p.x == 9.0, "attributes must stay writable"
assert not hasattr(p, "__dict__"), "instances must not have a per-object __dict__ (use __slots__)"
try:
    p.colour = "red"
except AttributeError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a slotted class refuses attributes that are not declared")
assert set(Particle.__slots__) == {"x", "y", "mass"}, "declare exactly x, y and mass in __slots__"

q.en: What does a normal Python object use to store its attributes?
What happens when you assign an attribute not listed in `__slots__`?

en: It is stored in the class
A class that adds fields at runtime

q.en: A subclass of a slotted class declares no `__slots__` of its own. What follows?

en: It is faster than the parent

q.en: Why did the lesson report memory measured with `tracemalloc`?

en: Because the saving depends on Python version and fields, so claims need measuring
Because slots only work with tracemalloc

under_the_hood.summary: A normal object stores attributes in a per-instance dict; __slots__ swaps that dict for fixed positions inside the object. The saving appears when you create very many small objects of the same shape.

steps.title: Instances own a dictionary
steps.body: When `Particle(1.0, 2.0, 0.5)` runs `self.x = x`, Python stores the name `'x'` and its value in that object's `__dict__`. Each instance therefore holds its own mapping, even though every particle uses the same three names.

steps.title: Slots fix the layout in the class
steps.body: `__slots__ = ('x', 'y', 'mass')` makes the class remember the three names once. Each instance then reserves three fixed positions after its header, and `self.x = x` writes straight into position 0, with no dictionary involved.

steps.title: The dict is gone
steps.body: With no `__dict__`, a slotted instance cannot grow new attributes. `p.colour = 'red'` raises `AttributeError`, which is why a misspelled field name now fails loudly instead of creating a stray attribute.

steps.title: What it saved, measured
steps.body: On Python 3.11, 100,000 three-attribute instances held about 10.4 MB as plain objects and about 6.4 MB with `__slots__` — roughly 104 against 64 bytes each. The exact figures depend on the version and the number of attributes, so measure yours.

steps.title: Where the saving disappears
steps.body: A subclass that does not declare `__slots__` regains a `__dict__`, so every class in the chain must declare its own. And adding slots to a class you create only a few times saves nothing noticeable while removing flexibility.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Plain objects pay for a dictionary each. For many small records of fixed shape, __slots__ removes it — about 40% less memory in our 3.11 measurement — at the price of no dynamic attributes.
